introduction-bringing-order-to-chaos.core: Without structure, incidents become chaos: everyone debugs, nobody coordinates and nobody communicates. Defined roles (Incident Commander, Ops Lead, Scribe, Liaison, SMEs) separate coordinating, fixing, recording and communicating.

first_principles.problem: Twenty engineers in a channel all try different fixes, two of them conflict, and leadership has no idea what's happening.
truths: Humans can't do every job at once under stress.
derivation: Have **one IC** who coordinates and decides.
An **Ops Lead** to direct the hands-on fixing.
A **Liaison** to handle communications; **SMEs** on demand.

analogy.title: A restaurant kitchen brigade
analogy.story: Head chef, line cooks and expediter each know their station, so the rush runs smoothly.
analogy.breaks: Small incidents may need just one person doing several roles, so scale it to severity.

example.title: A chaotic vs a structured incident
flow: Structured: IC assigns DB SME + rollback owner

check.q: Why separate the Incident Commander role from the people fixing?
check.a: Coordination needs a big-picture view that hands-on debugging prevents.

the-incident-commander-ic-the-conductor.core: The IC is the single source of authority. They set priorities, delegate tasks, make decisions and keep the response moving, but they don't debug. Like a conductor, they direct rather than play.

first_principles.problem: The most senior engineer takes charge but gets lost in logs, and nobody's steering.
truths: Someone must hold the whole picture.

analogy.title: An orchestra conductor
analogy.story: They don't play an instrument; they keep everyone in time and decide the tempo.
analogy.breaks: The IC can also be junior. The role needs process skill more than seniority.

example.title: IC instructions

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Every task has an owner and a deadline.

code.text:
IC: "Priya, you own rollback of api v2.3 — report back in 10 min.
Sam, check DB replica lag. Alex (Liaison), post status page update now.
Next sync at :15."

example.outcome: a steady hand steering the response.

check.q: Should the Incident Commander debug the system?
check.a: No. They coordinate and decide while others do the hands-on work.

the-art-of-the-handoff.core: Long incidents need IC rotation before fatigue degrades judgement. A formal handoff (state summary, open tasks, decisions, next steps, then an explicit 'you are now IC') transfers command without losing context.

first_principles.problem: After 6 hours, an exhausted IC makes poor decisions, and an informal swap loses track of who owns what.
truths: Context lives in people's heads unless written down.
Ambiguity about who's in charge is dangerous.
derivation: **Brief**: current state, impact, hypotheses, actions in flight.
**Explicitly transfer**: 'I am handing IC to Dana.'
**Announce** it in the channel and on the bridge.

analogy.title: A pilot handing over the controls
analogy.story: 'You have control.' 'I have control.' There's no ambiguity about who's flying.
analogy.breaks: Handoffs mid-crisis are risky, so pick a stable moment if you can.

example.title: A handoff template

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No lost context, and clear authority.

code.text:
Status: SEV1, payments degraded 40%
Mitigation: traffic shifted to us-west, partial
In flight: DB failover (Sam, ETA 20m), vendor ticket open
Decisions: no full rollback yet
Next sync: 14:30
"Dana, you are now IC." — "I am IC."

example.outcome: sustained, sharp command over long incidents.

check.q: What makes an IC handoff safe?
check.a: A structured briefing of state and open tasks, followed by an explicit, announced transfer of command.

the-supporting-cast-scribe-and-liaison.core: The Scribe records a timestamped timeline of events, decisions and actions (vital for the postmortem). The Liaison handles all communication with stakeholders, customers and executives, protecting responders from interruptions.

first_principles.problem: The IC is constantly interrupted by executives asking for updates, and afterwards nobody remembers what happened when.
derivation: **Scribe**: timestamps, actions, decisions, who did what.
**Liaison**: status page, exec briefings, support updates on a cadence.

analogy.title: A court stenographer and a press secretary
analogy.story: One records everything accurately; the other speaks to the public so the principals can work.
analogy.breaks: Tools (incident bots) can automate parts of the scribing, but someone still owns it.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: An accurate postmortem, and responders aren't interrupted.

code.text:
14:02 Alert: checkout 5xx > 5%
14:05 IC declared (Lee), SEV1
14:09 Hypothesis: deploy v2.3 — rollback started (Priya)
14:14 Liaison posted status page update
14:16 Errors back to baseline

check.q: Why have a dedicated Liaison during a major incident?
check.a: To handle stakeholder communication consistently and keep interruptions away from the IC and fixers.

the-fixers-operations-lead-and-smes.core: The Operations Lead directs the hands-on technical work and coordinates the SMEs (database, network, service owners) pulled in for specific expertise. The IC sets the what; Ops decides the how.

first_principles.problem: SMEs join the incident and start making changes independently, which conflicts with other fixes.
truths: Experts are needed only for parts of the problem.
derivation: The **Ops Lead** owns the technical plan and change control.
Release SMEs **once they're no longer needed**.

analogy.title: A surgical team
analogy.story: The lead surgeon directs while specialists (anaesthetist, cardiologist) join for their part.
analogy.breaks: In small incidents the IC and Ops Lead can be the same person.

example.title: Coordinated changes
flow: Ops Lead: 'Network SME, check LB health'
'DB SME, hold — don't fail over yet'

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No conflicting changes, and it's clear what fixed it.

check.q: Why announce changes before making them during an incident?
check.a: To prevent conflicting actions and to know which change affected the system.

putting-it-all-together-the-ics-structur.core: The full picture: the IC leads; the Ops Lead and SMEs fix; the Scribe records; the Liaison communicates. Each has clear responsibilities, a reporting line and things they shouldn't do, scaled to the incident's severity.

first_principles.problem: Roles exist on paper, but people don't know their boundaries during a real incident.
truths: Structure must scale up and down.
derivation: **IC**: decides and coordinates, but doesn't debug.
**Ops Lead**: technical plan, not external comms.

analogy.title: A sports team's positions
analogy.story: Each player knows their position and doesn't wander, which is why the team plays well under pressure.
analogy.breaks: Rigid roles in small incidents waste people, so combine roles at low severity.

example.title: Roles by severity

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The right amount of structure every time.

example.outcome: a role system that scales with severity.

check.q: What should the Liaison avoid doing?
check.a: Speculating about causes or timelines that haven't been confirmed, as well as hands-on fixing.
